title: Decision Rights in Human–AI Organizations: A matched simulation of agent autonomy, human accountability, and review workload
description: As AI agents acquire execution capabilities, organizations face the problem of delegating routine actions while preserving accountability and limiting review costs. This paper develops a four-tier decision-rights model and examines its operation in a synthetic business-workflow sandbox. A matched simulation of 1,000 cases compares unrestricted decision rights, blanket review of mutations, and risk-tiered governance combined with a trusted operation mandate. Under the default assumptions, the combined configuration produces zero trials with unauthorized persistent mutations, compared with 268 and 5 in the alternatives; the corresponding counts of changed records are 0, 376 and 7. It routes 341 cases to review, compared with 785 under blanket review. A post-hoc ablation yields 6 affected trials for tier rules alone and 190 for the mandate alone. Sensitivity analysis identifies residual vulnerabilities under modeled reviewer error. A reduced-form loss model derives the accuracy threshold below which discretionary review is economically preferable. A separate four-arm gateway smoke test evaluates 20 existing fixtures (80 policy evaluations) and passes 13 software unit tests. The test isolates mandate enforcement from review routing in the implementation. These results concern synthetic workflows and software behavior; live model performance and actual human review remain unmeasured.
